extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and the inductive sciences
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing principles about the nature, origin, and status of axioms, definitions, and hypotheses in geometry and the inductive sciences; focuses on what counts as evidence, necessity, and admissible simplification in scientific reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must relate to real objects
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis framed for the purpose of scientific inquiry must relate to something which has real existence; there can be no science respecting nonentities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and simplifying assumptions are permissible only insofar as they relate to real objects. Do not adopt hypotheses that ascribe to an object any property which it does not have; liberty extends only to slight exaggerations of actual properties or suppression of other properties for convenience. Restore omitted properties when their presence or absence would materially change conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible definitions must match conceivable conception
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition, to be admissible, must necessarily refer to and agree with some conception which we can distinctly frame in our thoughts (e.g., straight lines must be those by which angles are contained, triangles bounded, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or creating definitions, ensure they correspond to a clear mental conception and to real instances. Avoid definitions that are disconnected from any representable or observable conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions/hypotheses from axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some first principles are involved in definitions (hypotheses) while others are axioms; axioms differ by being true without any mixture of hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing foundational principles, classify which are definitional/suppositional (convenient fictions) and which are axiomatic (general propositions accepted as true without hypothesis). This affects how strongly conclusions can be regarded as reflecting reality versus following from chosen suppositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include axioms among first principles of geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to admit among the first principles both axioms and definitions; some axioms are fundamental truths not capable of being demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that not all foundational propositions can be reduced to definitions or proven; treat such indemonstrable yet foundational axioms as legitimate premises of geometric reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms are experimental truths (generalizations from observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ground of our belief in axioms is that they are experimental truths; generalizations from observation (e.g., 'Two straight lines cannot inclose a space' is an induction from the evidence of our senses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of axiomatic truth by appeal to their empirical origins and the ubiquity of confirming observations rather than assuming an innate a priori source. Consider observational frequency and the correspondence between mental images and sensory experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of deductive conclusions is conditional on hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is affirmed that the conclusions of geometry are necessary truths, the necessity consists only in this, that they correctly follow from the suppositions from which they are deduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between logical necessity (derivation from premises) and metaphysical necessity (truth independent of premises). When assessing the force of geometric conclusions, note the conditionality on the chosen assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental intuition depends on prior experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity to recognise geometric truths by merely thinking of them rests on the fact that our mental pictures exactly resemble sensations and that in acquiring the idea we have already learned the necessary facts by experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept mere conceivability as evidence of a priori truth; require demonstration that the mental intuition derives from prior, representative sensory experience. Use the equivalence of accurate mental diagrams and real observation as legitimate experimental ground only when that equivalence is empirically justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivableness is not proof of impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The incapacity to conceive the negation of a proposition (inconceivableness) is often due to habitual association and past mental history, not to an inherent impossibility of the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When someone appeals to inconceivableness to establish necessity, check historical and psychological contingency: past experience and habit can make truths appear inconceivable. Avoid treating present inability to imagine a possibility as conclusive proof that it is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow mental diagrams as experimental instances when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometrical forms have the capacity of being painted in the imagination with a distinctness equal to reality; pictures, if sufficiently accurate, exhibit the properties which would be manifested by the realities at one instant, and thus may serve as subjects of geometrical experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mental experimentation (imagined diagrams) as valid evidence only insofar as there is established practice that such pictures faithfully represent the real properties under study. Be cautious where dynamic mutual actions or non-geometric properties matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore omitted properties when they materially affect truth
rubrics_metrics.description: We may, for scientific convenience, feign objects divested of all properties except those material to our purpose, but we are under the obligation of restoring suppressed properties whenever and in as far as their presence or absence would make any material difference in the truth of our conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing simplifications, explicitly identify omitted factors and check whether including them would alter results. Avoid overextending conclusions drawn from idealized models without correction for omitted real-world properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some axioms admit demonstration, others do not
rubrics_metrics.description: Though some axioms of Euclid might be exhibited in the form of definitions or be proved by imaginary superposition, there remain two or three fundamental truths not capable of being demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which foundational propositions can be reduced to demonstrable claims and which must be accepted as indemonstrable. Different handling (justification vs. acceptance) is required in reasoning and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical confirmation strengthens axioms despite lack of infinite observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where direct observation to infinity is impossible, repeated and ubiquitous confirmation by experience supplies overwhelming grounds for belief in axioms (e.g., seeing two intersecting straight lines diverge at every observed instance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When direct empirical proof is unattainable (e.g., propositions about infinite extension), rely on the accumulation and ubiquity of finite observations together with reasoned extrapolation and validated equivalence between imagination and observation to justify acceptance.
